claim: The human kinome comprises 538 kinases.
source: The human kinome comprises 538 kinases playing essential functions by catalyzing protein phosphorylation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citation to Manning et al., 2002b in the introduction.

claim: 456 epitope-tagged kinases, representing 85% of the human kinome, were expressed in HeLa cells and imaged by immunofluorescent microscopy.
source: 456 epitope-tagged kinases, representing 85% of the human kinome, were expressed in HeLa cells and imaged by immunofluorescent microscopy under a similar condition.
evidence: This is a primary methodological claim directly stated in the abstract and supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: KA revealed kinase family-enriched subcellular localizations.
source: KA revealed kinase family-enriched subcellular localizations and discovered a collection of new kinase localizations at mitochondria, plasma membrane, extracellular space, and other structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 1F and 1G showing family-based enrichment patterns.

claim: KA discovered a collection of new kinase localizations at mitochondria, plasma membrane, extracellular space, and other structures.
source: KA revealed kinase family-enriched subcellular localizations and discovered a collection of new kinase localizations at mitochondria, plasma membrane, extracellular space, and other structures.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 5, demonstrating novel localizations.

claim: KA demonstrated the role of liquid-liquid phase separation in formation of kinase condensates.
source: Furthermore, KA demonstrated the role of liquid-liquid phase separation in formation of kinase condensates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing hexanediol sensitivity and fusion events.

claim: MOK is a mitochondrial kinase.
source: Identification of MOK as a mitochondrial kinase revealed its function in cristae dynamics, respiration, and oxidative stress response.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experiments including co-staining, fractionation, and functional assays shown in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: MOK functions in cristae dynamics, respiration, and oxidative stress response.
source: Identification of MOK as a mitochondrial kinase revealed its function in cristae dynamics, respiration, and oxidative stress response.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy, Seahorse analysis, and ROS measurements in Figure 7.

claim: The kinome is encoded by about 2% of the human genome.
source: The kinome, encoded by about 2% of the human genome, is one of the largest superfamilies of homologous proteins consisting of 538 kinases (Manning et al., 2002b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Manning et al., 2002b.

claim: Kinases catalyze the transfer of γ-phosphate of ATP to the alcohol groups (on Ser and Thr) or phenolic groups (on Tyr) of proteins.
source: These enzymes catalyze the transfer of γ-phosphate of ATP to the alcohol groups (on Ser and Thr) or phenolic groups (on Tyr) of proteins to generate phosphate monoesters.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about kinase function.

claim: Protein phosphorylation can alter substrate protein activity, subcellular localization, and interacting proteins.
source: As a consequence, the substrate protein could be altered in many ways, such as activity, subcellular localization, and interacting proteins (Cohen, 2002; Manning et al., 2002a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cohen, 2002 and Manning et al., 2002a.

claim: Mutation and dysregulation of protein kinases are causal to many diseases such as cancer.
source: Mutation and dysregulation of protein kinases are causal to many diseases such as cancer (Greenman et al., 2007; Lahiry et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Greenman et al., 2007 and Lahiry et al., 2010.

claim: Kinases are among the most important targets for precision medicine.
source: Kinases are also among the most important targets for precision medicine (Klaeger et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Klaeger et al., 2017 and Zhang et al., 2009.

claim: 464 protein kinase-encoding plasmids were constructed, representing 86.2% of the human kinome.
source: 464 protein kinase-encoding plasmids were got (Supplementary file 1), representing 86.2% of the human kinome, and covering each family similarly (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by the data in Figure 1A.

claim: 95.1% of genes in the library are of human origin, and the rest are of mouse or rat origins.
source: 95.1% of genes in the library are of human origin, and the rest are of mouse or rat origins (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 46.8% of clones have Flag tag, 46.5% have tandem HA/Flag tags, 3.4% have HA tag, 2.4% have Myc tag, and 0.9% have GFP tag.
source: All clones are epitope-tagged, with 46.8% in Flag tag, 46.5% in tandem HA/Flag tags, 3.4% in HA tag, 2.4% in Myc tag, and 0.9% in GFP tag.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 54.7% of the clones have epitope tags on the N-terminal, and 45.3% of clones are tagged on the C-terminal.
source: 54.7% of the clones have epitope tags on the amino (N)-terminal, and 45.3% of clones are tagged on the carboxyl (C)-terminal (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 37% of plasmids showed high level of expression, 58.5% had medium or low expression, and 4.5% could not be detected.
source: By western blotting, 37% of plasmids showed high level of expression, 58.5% had medium or low expression, and 4.5% could not be detected (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the western blotting data summarized in Figure 1C.

claim: A total of 456 kinases were annotated, while the other 8 kinases were not detected.
source: A total of 456 kinases were annotated, while the other 8 kinases were not detected.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results from the imaging screen.

claim: About 50.2% of the kinome mainly localized in the cytosol, followed by 16.4% in nucleus, and 10.3% on plasma membrane.
source: In the initial screen, about 50.2% of the kinome mainly localized in the cytosol, followed by 16.4% in nucleus, and 10.3% on plasma membrane (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 77.5% of the STE family were in cytosol, significantly higher than other families.
source: 77.5% of the STE (homologues of yeast Ste7, Ste11, and Ste20 kinases) family were in cytosol, significantly higher than other families (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CMGC, atypical, and CAMK families were more enriched for nuclear kinases, 39.0, 34.5, and 30.2%, respectively.
source: On the other hand, CMGC (CDK, MAPK, GSK3, and CLK kinases), atypical, and calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinases (CAMK) families were more enriched for nuclear kinases, 39.0, 34.5, and 30.2%, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis of family distributions.

claim: The TK family was enriched for kinases on the plasma membrane, largely due to the receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) subfamily.
source: The TK family was enriched for kinases on the plasma membrane, largely due to the receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) subfamily.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis and is consistent with known biology of RTKs.

claim: The AGC family was overrepresented on the plasma membrane reflecting their functions in relaying extracellular signals.
source: The AGC (family of protein kinases A, G, and C) family was also overrepresented on the plasma membrane reflecting their functions in relaying extracellular signals.
evidence: This is supported by the data and known functions of AGC kinases.

claim: Most mitochondrial kinases were in the atypical kinase family.
source: Most mitochondrial kinases were in the atypical kinase family.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis of family distributions.

claim: The RGC and PKL families were largely formed by ER- and Golgi-localized kinases.
source: Finally, the receptor guanylate cyclase (RGC) and PKL families were largely formed by ER- and Golgi-localized kinases.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis of family distributions.

claim: KA annotated 18 kinases on top of COMPARTMENTS and HPA.
source: 6 kinases were not covered by any of the three resources, and KA annotated 18 kinases on top of COMPARTMENTS and HPA (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Six kinases were annotated for the first time: STK32C, SBK2, STKLD1, TSSK1B, NME8, and SRPK3, which were all cytosolic in KA.
source: Manual literature search eliminated 12 kinases with at least one report, resulting in 6 kinases annotated for the first time, including STK32C, SBK2, STKLD1, TSSK1B, NME8, and SRPK3, which were all cytosolic in KA (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by literature search and the imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 71.2% of kinases documented by both KA and COMPARTMENTS matched with one of the high-confidence localizations in COMPARTMENTS.
source: Among 337 kinases documented by both KA and COMPARTMENTS, 71.2% matched with one of the high-confidence localizations in COMPARTMENTS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 74.8% of localizations were consistent between revised KA and COMPARTMENTS.
source: Comparison between revised KA and COMPARTMENTS revealed 74.8% localizations were consistent (Figure 2C and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: KA uniquely annotated 103 kinase localizations different from other databases.
source: Furthermore, KA uniquely annotated 103 kinase localizations different from other databases (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: These unique localizations were largely unpredictable by mainstream subcellular localization prediction tools such as WoLF PSORT and YLoc.
source: Importantly, these localization were largely unpredictable by main stream subcellular localization prediction tools such as WoLF PSORT and YLoc (Briesemeister et al., 2010; Horton et al., 2007; Figure 2H and Supplementary file 6), suggesting new localization mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by the prediction analysis shown in Figure 2H and citations to the prediction tools.

claim: Seven kinases exhibited novel plasma membrane localization in KA: RPS6KA2, BRSK2, NIM1K, CSNK1G3, NLK, MAPK11, and FRK.
source: Seven kinases exhibited novel plasma membrane localization in KA (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data in Figure 3A and fractionation data in Figure 3B.

claim: RPS6KA2, BRSK2, NIM1K, CSNK1G3, and NLK were mainly membranous, while MAPK11 and FRK were partially in membrane fractions.
source: Cellular fraction confirmed that RPS6KA2, BRSK2, NIM1K, CSNK1G3, and NLK were mainly membranous, while MAPK11 and FRK were partially in membrane fractions (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the fractionation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: POMK has an ER-related function in phosphorylating glycosylation-specific O-mannose and is mutated in dystroglycanopathies.
source: POMK has an ER-related function in phosphorylating glycosylation-specific O-mannose and is mutated in a neuromuscular disorder dystroglycanopathies (Di Costanzo et al., 2014; Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Di Costanzo et al., 2014 and Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013.

claim: POMK localizes to the ER.
source: By co-expression with GFP-tagged SEC61B, an ER resident protein, we confirmed the ER localization of POMK (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the co-localization data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: SGK3 was enriched in vesicles around the Golgi, with lower expression in the Golgi itself.
source: SGK3 was enriched in vesicles around the Golgi, with lower expression in the Golgi itself (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: SGK3 colocalized with endosomal marker EEA1.
source: In addition, SGK3 colocalized with endosomal marker EEA1 as previously reported (Xu et al., 2001; Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the co-localization data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and citation to Xu et al., 2001.

claim: SGK3 is secreted to the extracellular space.
source: Interestingly, SGK3, but not other kinases examined, could be immunoprecipitated from culture medium (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), indicating it was secreted, although at a much lower level than FAM20C.
evidence: This is supported by the immunoprecipitation data from culture medium shown in Figure 3E.

claim: SGK3 secretion is not blocked by brefeldin A.
source: First, treatment of cells with brefeldin A (BFA), an inhibitor of ER/Golgi‐trafficking (Misumi et al., 1986), blocked secretion of FAM20C, but not SGK3 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by the BFA treatment data shown in Figure 3E and citation to Misumi et al., 1986.

claim: SGK3 is enriched in exosomes.
source: Second, when exosomes were sedimented from medium by ultracentrifugation, SGK3 but not FAM20C was enriched in the pellet fraction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the ultracentrifugation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: SGK3 is a new exosomal kinase.
source: Thus, SGK3 is a new exosomal kinase, which may mediate cellular communication with the microenvironment.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing SGK3 in exosomes.

claim: MAP4K3 localizes to tubule-like structures that colocalize with microtubules and ER.
source: We found MAP4K3 in tubule-like structures in KA. Co-staining indicated that MAP4K3 structures were colocalizing with a small fraction of microtubules (Figure 3F). These tubules were also non-overlapping with lysosomes even in amino acid starvation condition or in cells treated with vacuolin-1, a chemical that cause lysosome fusion and enlargement (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E). However, MAP4K3 tubules were overlapping with ER (Figure 3F), which was confirmed by super-resolution microscopy (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by the co-staining data shown in Figure 3F and 3G.

claim: MAP4K3 tubules are obvious in A549, Du 145, and H460 cells, all of which have mutation of the LKB1 gene.
source: Interestingly, MAP4K3 tubules were also obvious in A549, Du 145, and H460 cells, all of which, as well as HeLa cells, have mutation of the LKB1 gene, an upstream regulator of mTOR (Corradetti et al., 2004; Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 3H and citation to Corradetti et al., 2004.

claim: MAP4K3 is mainly cytoplasmic with some small puncta in LKB1-wildtype COS-7, U-2 OS, and MCF10A cells.
source: Surprisingly, MAP4K3 were mainly cytoplasmic with some small puncta in LKB1-wildtype COS-7, U-2 OS, and MCF10A cells.
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Restoration of LKB1 expression in H460 cells markedly inhibited MAP4K3 tubules.
source: Furthermore, restoration of LKB1 expression in H460 cells markedly inhibited MAP4K3 tubules (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: VRK3, BRD3, CDK8, CDKL3, TRIM24, and RPS6KA4 were enriched in periphery regions of the nucleus.
source: For instance, TRIB1, CDK10, CDK7, HASPIN, and STK17A were evenly distributed in nucleoplasm, while VRK3, BRD3, CDK8, CDKL3, TRIM24, and RPS6KA4 were enriched in periphery regions of the nucleus (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: All six nuclear peripheral kinases were found within the nuclear boundary.
source: By high-resolution microscopy, all six nuclear peripheral kinases were found within the nuclear boundary (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the high-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: VRK3 phosphorylated nuclear envelope protein barrier-to-autointegration factor (BAF), thus played a role in cell cycle regulation.
source: Interestingly, it was reported that VRK3 phosphorylated nuclear envelope protein barrier-to-autointegration factor (BAF), thus played a role in cell cycle regulation (Park et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Park et al., 2015.

claim: CDK13 and STK19 were found in structures reminiscent of nucleoli.
source: Two kinases CDK13 and STK19 were found in structures reminiscent of nucleoli (Figure 4A), which was confirmed by co-staining with a nucleolar protein UTP25 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting their potential roles in ribosome biogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 4A and co-staining data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Nuclear puncta formed by TRIB3 and HIPK2, as well as cytoplasmic puncta of BMP2K and CIT were largely eliminated by 1,6-hexanediol.
source: Nuclear puncta formed by TRIB3 and HIPK2, as well as cytoplasmic puncta of BMP2K and CIT were largely eliminated by Hex (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the hexanediol treatment data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Time-lapse live-cell imaging revealed frequent puncta movements and fusion events for TRIB3, HIPK2, and BMP2K.
source: Time-lapse live-cell imaging revealed frequent puncta movements and fusion events for TRIB3, HIPK2, and BMP2K, demonstrating their dynamic and liquid-like properties (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: HIPK2 and BMP2K have prion-like regions overlapping with IDRs.
source: Importantly, among all kinases analyzed, HIPK2, and BMP2K uniquely have prion-like regions overlapping with IDRs, which are largely devoid of charged residues, but enriched for polar residues, and are frequently involved in LLPS (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: This is supported by the sequence analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Deletion of IDRs eliminated puncta of TRIB3 and BMP2K.
source: Furthermore, deletion of IDRs eliminated puncta of TRIB3 and BMP2K, supporting IDR-mediated LLPS (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by the deletion mutant data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Endogenous BMP2K forms cytoplasmic puncta that are eliminated by hexanediol treatment.
source: To determine whether BMP2K could form puncta through LLPS on endogenous expression level, we generated BMP2K 3xHA tag knock-in HeLa cells through CRISPR/Cas9-mediated recombination (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I). Successful knock-in was confirmed by western blotting (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J). Two types of BMP2K patterns were found, in cytoplasmic puncta or both in cytoplasmic puncta and nuclei (Figure 4F). Nuclear BMP2K was not observed in overexpression expression experiments and could be due to a different isoform. Importantly, cytoplasmic puncta of endogenous BMP2K were also eliminated by Hex treatment (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by the knock-in cell data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: KA recorded 22 kinases with some level of mitochondrial localization.
source: KA recorded 22 kinases with some level of mitochondrial localization (Figure 5A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 14 of the 22 mitochondrial kinases have been documented in mitochondrial proteome database MitoCarta2.0.
source: 14 of them have been documented in mitochondrial proteome database MitoCarta2.0 (Calvo et al., 2016; Figure 5A), among which 6 were confirmed by co-staining with mitochondrial marker translocase of outer membrane 20 (TOM20) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with MitoCarta2.0 database and citation to Calvo et al., 2016.

claim: FASTK transcribed from an alternative start codon missing N-terminal 34 amino acids was mitochondrial.
source: It was reported that FASTK transcribed from an alternative start codon missing N-terminal 34 amino acids was mitochondrial (Jourdain et al., 2015), which we could confirm (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and citation to Jourdain et al., 2015.

claim: KA found eight new mitochondrial kinases.
source: Remarkably, we found eight new mitochondrial kinases, which were confirmed by co-staining with TOM20 (Figure 5A, C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the co-staining data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: KA revealed five new mitochondrial kinases: MOK, LIMK2, PKN3, PRKCH, and TNK1.
source: Taken together, KA revealed five new mitochondrial kinases, MOK, LIMK2, PKN3, PRKCH, and TNK1.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings after comparison with databases.

claim: Endogenous MOK is present in mitochondria.
source: Endogenous MOK was present in mitochondria. MOK 3x Flag knock-in HeLa cells were fractionated and examined by western blotting. W: whole cell lysate; N: nucleus; MI: mitochondria; C: cytosol. Lamin A/C, MT-CO2, and Actin are nuclear, mitochondrial, and cytosolic markers, respectively. Equal loading was achieved by normalizing to the same number of cells. Arrowheads indicate MOK (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the fractionation data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: MOK, TNK1, and RPS6KA6 signals were wrapped around by TOM20, indicating transportation into mitochondria.
source: Using 3D structured illumination microscopy (3D-SIM), we found that signals of MOK, TNK1, and RPS6KA6 were wrapped around by TOM20, an OMM protein (Figure 6A), indicating transportation into mitochondria.
evidence: This is supported by the 3D-SIM data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: LIMK2 was in puncta partially colocalizing with TOM20, indicating that LIMK2 decorated the outer surface of mitochondria.
source: In contrast, LIMK2 was in puncta partially colocalizing with TOM20, indicating that LIMK2 decorated the outer surface of mitochondria.
evidence: This is inferred from the 3D-SIM data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: MOK2 is imported into mitochondria.
source: MOK2 is imported into mitochondria. Transfected HeLa cells were fixed and permeabilized with digitonin or Triton X-100 before staining.
evidence: This is supported by the differential permeabilization data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: MOK is not a mitochondrial membrane protein.
source: MOK is not a mitochondrial membrane protein. Mitochondria purified from transfected HeLa cells were incubated in indicated buffers, and then centrifuged. Supernatants (S) and pellets (P) were analyzed by western blotting. Equal loading was achieved by normalizing to the same number of cells.
evidence: This is supported by the extraction data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: MOK is an IMS protein.
source: MOK is an IMS protein. COS-7 cells transfected with MOK2-GFP were imaged by Hessian SIM. MitoTracker Red marked inner membrane (IMM) and co-transfected HSP60-mCherry marked matrix.
evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of evidence including permeabilization, extraction, and super-resolution imaging shown in Figures 6B, 6C, and 6D.

claim: MOK2 has better mitochondrial localization than MOK1.
source: MOK2 has better mitochondrial localization than MOK1. HeLa cells were transfected with full-length (FL) or kinase domain (KD) of MOK1 and MOK2. Cells with mitochondrial MOK were quantified. Data is represented as mean ± SD; n = 3 independent experiments, two-tailed Student's t test; n = 100 cells were analyzed in each experiment.
evidence: This is supported by the quantification data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Two peptides 53–103 and 301–330 of MOK2 mediated the mitochondrial localization of MOK.
source: Therefore, two peptides 53–103 and 301–330 of MOK2 mediated the mitochondrial localization of MOK (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the deletion mutant analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of TOM20 but not TOM70 blocked mitochondrial localization of MOK.
source: shRNA-mediated knockdown of precursor receptor TOM20 but not TOM70 blocked mitochondrial localization of MOK, suggesting TOM20 as a receptor for MOK importing (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the knockdown data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Knockdown of TIM23, TIM17A, and TIM50 eliminated mitochondrial MOK.
source: Furthermore, knockdown of TIM23, TIM17A, and TIM50 in the same complex, but not TIM22 and TIM9, eliminated mitochondrial MOK (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by the knockdown data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Knockdown of HSPA9 suppressed MOK mitochondrial localization.
source: Knockdown of HSPA9, which is responsible for translocation of matrix protein downstream of the TIM23 complex, also suppressed MOK mitochondrial localization (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by the knockdown data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: MOK and its kinase domain physically interacted with TOM20 and TIM23.
source: Nevertheless, by co-immunoprecipitation, we confirmed that MOK and its kinase domain physically interacted with TOM20 and TIM23 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by the co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: MOK is an IMS protein imported by a TOM20-TIM23-dependent mechanism independent of classical mitochondrial importing signal.
source: Taken together, MOK is an IMS protein imported by a TOM20-TIM23-dependent mechanism independent of classical mitochondrial importing signal.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: The number of cristae markedly reduced in MOK KO cells.
source: Electron microscopy revealed that while mitochondria length remained normal, the number of cristae markedly reduced in MOK KO cells (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: This is supported by the electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: The cristae defect in MOK KO cells could be rescued by re-expression of MOK1 or MOK2.
source: This defect could be rescued by re-expression of MOK1 or MOK2.
evidence: This is supported by the rescue experiment data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Oxygen consumption rates for both basal respiration and ATP production were reduced in MOK KO cells.
source: Cristae have a pivotal role in generating ATP (Cogliati et al., 2013). Indeed, oxygen consumption rates (OCRs) for both basal respiration and ATP production were reduced in MOK KO cells (Figure 7C, D).
evidence: This is supported by the Seahorse analysis data shown in Figure 7C and 7D, and citation to Cogliati et al., 2013.

claim: Re-expression of MOK2 rescued mitochondrial respiration in MOK KO cells.
source: Re-expression of MOK2 rescued mitochondrial respiration, while rescue by MOK1 was statistically insignificant.
evidence: This is supported by the rescue experiment data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Knockout of MOK reduced cellular ATP level.
source: Consistently, knockout of MOK reduced cellular ATP level, which could be rescued by MOK2, but not MOK1 (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by the ATP measurement data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: ROS level was higher in MOK KO cells under basal condition.
source: Under basal condition, ROS level was higher in MOK KO cells, but was rescued by expression of MOK1 and MOK2 (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by the ROS measurement data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Oxidative stress induced by diamide caused more apoptosis in MOK KO cells.
source: Furthermore, oxidative stress induced by diamide caused more apoptosis in MOK KO cells (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by the apoptosis assay data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: MOK2 was kinase inactive.
source: Using in vitro autophosphorylation as an assay, we confirmed that MOK2 was kinase inactive (Figure 7—figure supplement 1I), consistent with its incomplete kinase domain.
evidence: This is supported by the in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1I.

claim: MOK played a functional role in mitochondria in an activity-independent manner.
source: Nevertheless, MOK2 not only had better mitochondrial localization than MOK1, but also rescued mitochondrial structure and functions in KO cells. Thus, MOK played a functional role in mitochondria in an activity-independent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that kinase-inactive MOK2 rescued mitochondrial defects.

claim: About 20% of proteins co-purified with MOK were mitochondrial proteins.
source: Mass spectrometry revealed that about 20% of proteins co-purified with MOK were mitochondrial proteins, including mitochondrial ribosomal proteins, solute carriers, oxidative phosphorylation-related proteins, and chaperones (Figure 7—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is supported by the TAP-MS data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: MOK interacts with ATAD3A, SLC25A13, and SLC25A11.
source: Immunoprecipitation confirmed interactions of MOK with IMM protein ATAD3A and solute carriers SLC25A13 and SLC25A11 (Figure 7I, Figure 7—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is supported by the co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: ATAD3A has important functions in mitochondrial structure dynamics.
source: ATAD3A spans OMM and IMM with two transmembrane regions (Gilquin et al., 2010), and has important functions in mitochondrial structure dynamics (Cooper et al., 2017; He et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gilquin et al., 2010; Cooper et al., 2017; He et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2019.

claim: ATAD3A knockdown cells exhibited reduced cristae number.
source: Indeed, ATAD3A knockdown cells also exhibited reduced cristae number (Figure 7J, K, Figure 7—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: This is supported by the electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7J and 7K.

claim: 19.1% (87/456) of kinases had only one localization.
source: 19.1% (87/456) of kinases had only one localization, 72.4% (330/456) had a specific major localization (score ≥5), and 8.5% (39/456) were multi-localizing.
evidence: This is a summary of the localization data from KA.

claim: 72.4% (330/456) of kinases had a specific major localization (score ≥5).
source: 19.1% (87/456) of kinases had only one localization, 72.4% (330/456) had a specific major localization (score ≥5), and 8.5% (39/456) were multi-localizing.
evidence: This is a summary of the localization data from KA.

claim: 8.5% (39/456) of kinases were multi-localizing.
source: 19.1% (87/456) of kinases had only one localization, 72.4% (330/456) had a specific major localization (score ≥5), and 8.5% (39/456) were multi-localizing.
evidence: This is a summary of the localization data from KA.

claim: 38.2% of specific nuclear kinases had uneven localizations with puncta in varying size under overexpression condition.
source: In KA, we found that 38.2% of specific nuclear kinases had uneven localizations with puncta in varying size under overexpression condition.
evidence: This is a summary of the observation from KA imaging data.

claim: BMP2K was mutated in the IDR in developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) and high myopia diseases.
source: Interestingly, BMP2K was mutated in the IDR in developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) and high myopia diseases (Liu et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2017), suggesting functional roles of LLPS in BMP2K regulation and functions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2009 and Zhao et al., 2017.

claim: The mRNA level of MOK is much higher in spermatocytes and round spermatids compared with other tissues.
source: Compared with other tissues, the mRNA level of MOK is much higher in spermatocytes and round spermatids.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion but the source of this data is not explicitly cited.

claim: MOK expression is elevated in cancer, such as in cholangiocarcinoma and skin cutaneous melanoma.
